result.reason: The passage is the Mishnah text itself—presenting the ruling about the shepherd touching a dead fetus in the womb and the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili—which is precisely what the 'Mishnah: Fetus Status' prose section introduces and discusses.

All three items constitute the Gemara's explanation of the tanna kamma's reasoning via kal vachomer (item 1), its extension to non-kosher animals via a verse and hekesh (item 2), and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's counter-reasoning (item 3) — exactly the content described in candidate 3 ('Kal VaChomer Logic'), which introduces Rav Chisda's kal vachomer and the two-step argument, while the current placement under 'Hekesh: Kosher/Non-Kosher' (index 7) skips over the earlier steps that these items actually represent.

All four items continue the same chain of hoof-based objections and responses (kalut b'mei para, para b'mei gamal, kalut b'mei kelutah, and chazir b'mei chazirta) that candidate 2's prose explicitly describes, including the rav achtva'i bar ami objection at the end which candidate 2 anticipates and candidate 3 picks up afterward.

Both items together constitute Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's derivation from the verse — item 1 cites the verse and item 2 raises and resolves the question about its omission of kosher animals — which is precisely what candidate 1's prose ('Pasuk Omission Analysis') describes, including the question 'does only the corpse of a non-kosher animal cause tumah.'
The passage asks why Rabbi Yitzchak's verse is needed given Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's derivation, which is precisely what section 2 ('Purpose of Hooves Verse') describes in its prose.

The passage is the baraita of Rabbi Yonatan speaking to Ben Azzai about what we have learned regarding the tumah of carcasses of kosher/non-kosher behemah and non-kosher chayah, which is precisely what the 'Yonatan & Ben Azzai' section's prose describes.

The passage quotes the question 'we did not yet learn about a carcass of a kosher undomesticated animal, from where is it derived' along with Ben Azzai's cited verse answer, which corresponds directly to the 'Gap: Kosher Chaya' section's prose describing Rabbi Yonatan asking Ben Azzai 'nevelat chayah tehorah lo lamadnu—minayin' and Ben Azzai's response with that same verse.

The passage contains Rabbi Yonatan's rejection of Ben Azzai's drasha (explaining that 'b'chol hachayah' not 'v'chol chayah' limits the verse to paw-walkers) and Ben Azzai's follow-up question about Rabbi Yishmael — both of which are described in candidate 0's prose about Rabbi Yonatan rejecting the drasha, which concludes with the question about Rabbi Yishmael's view.

All three items together present Rabbi Yishmael's inclusion principle (chayah bichlal behemah and behemah bichlal chayah) with its full derivation and the concluding lament, but the core content of items 1-2 — deriving that behemah and chayah are interchangeable terms — matches the 'Inclusion Principle' heading's prose about Rabbi Yishmael's hermeneutic principle more precisely than the 'Application to Categories' heading, even though item 3's lament fits heading 2; the passage forms one continuous unit best housed under heading 0 where the principle itself is explained.
